headline: No shared execution or data channels are exposed; the main residual risk is low prompt-injection and leakage from manual copy-paste between pdf.js and python-cheatsheet.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: pdf.js can run browsers and process PDF files, while python-cheatsheet is documentation-only with no clipboard, stdin/stdout, MCP, or filesystem surfaces. No default machine channel is documented, so prompt injection would require manual copy-paste or an external bridge. That makes the pathway possible but unusual and limited.
conditions: IF an operator copies PDF-derived text from pdf.js into python-cheatsheet prompts or notes, injection becomes possible.
IF an external shared channel is added between the two agents, attacker-controlled PDF content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Avoid copy-pasting raw PDF text into the writing agent.
Strip instructions from extracted PDF text before reuse.
Use a fixed prompt template for any handoff.
Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for transferred text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: pdf.js touches PDF documents and has browser-based test tooling, but it has network egress set to none. python-cheatsheet has no file, clipboard, stdin/stdout, or screen-capture surfaces and touches no data classes. With no shared workspace or outbound channel documented, leakage is limited to unusual manual transfer of document contents.
conditions: IF PDF contents are manually transferred from pdf.js into python-cheatsheet outputs, document data can leak.
IF a shared filesystem is introduced outside the profiles, leakage risk increases.
mitigations: Do not paste PDF contents into the writing agent.
Redact sensitive fields before handoff.
Use separate storage locations for each agent.
Review outputs for accidental quotation of source PDFs.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: pdf.js has no filesystem write, git, shell, or network mutation capability in the profile, and python-cheatsheet explicitly lacks write_filesystem, modify_git_state, execute_shell, and spawn_subprocesses. With no overlapping write surface, there is no plausible capability conflict pathway.
conditions: IF either profile is expanded to include shared writable storage, conflict risk would need reassessment.
mitigations: Keep both agents read-only.
Avoid placing them on the same mutable workspace.
Do not grant git or shell privileges.
Monitor for profile changes before deployment.

D_cascading_error.rationale: pdf.js can extract or render PDF content, and python-cheatsheet is a content-writing agent that could reuse that output. The profiles do not show a verification step or critical action authority, so the main risk is that pdf.js output becomes authoritative input for writing. That pathway exists in default use if an operator forwards text directly.
conditions: IF pdf.js output is forwarded into python-cheatsheet without human verification, errors can cascade into written content.
IF the writing agent is asked to cite or summarize extracted PDF text, it may preserve upstream mistakes.
mitigations: Verify extracted facts against the original PDF.
Require a human review step before writing.
Mark PDF-derived text as untrusted input.
Separate extraction and drafting tasks.
requires-engineering: add automated citation checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no secrets, OAuth scopes, or explicit residency/retention settings. The only compliance concern visible is that pdf.js processes PDF documents while python-cheatsheet is a reference writer, so any regulated content would rely on manual handling rather than a documented policy mismatch. The other agent is not cited separately because no distinct compliance surface is exposed.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into PDF documents and then copied into the writing agent, compliance review is required.
IF a residency or retention policy is added later, the pair must be re-evaluated.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workflows.
Document retention expectations for any copied text.
Keep audit logs of manual transfers.
Use de-identified examples for drafting.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for sensitive documents.
